{{Short description|German physicist (born 1961)}}
{{Primary sources|date=July 2023}}
'''Jens Horst Gundlach''' (born 1961 in [[Würzburg]]) is a German physicist.

==Biography==
His father was Gerd Gundlach, a biochemistry professor in  [[Gießen]]. Jens Gundlach studied physics at the [[University of Mainz]] with ''Vordiplom'' (intermediate ''[[Diplom]]'') in 1982 and ''Diplom'' in 1986. After the ''Vordiplom'' he studied for a year in Seattle at the [[University of Washington]]. He received his doctorate there in 1990 under the supervision of Kurt Snover (1943–2021) with a dissertation entitled ''Shapes of excited rotating medium-mass nuclei determined from giant dipole resonance decays''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jens H. Gundlach|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=115237}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Kurt Snover|newspaper=The Seattle Times|date=January 2, 2022|url=https://obituaries.seattletimes.com/obituary/kurt-snover-1084083914}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1080/10619127.2022.2029319|title=In Memoriam: Kurt A. Snover (1943–2021) |year=2022 |last1=Kicińska-Habior |first1=Marta |journal=Nuclear Physics News |volume=32 |issue=1 |page=39 |s2cid=247980074 |doi-access= |bibcode=2022NPNew..32a..39K }}</ref> As a postdoc he was a research associate under the supervision of [[Eric Adelberger]] and [[Blayne Heckel]] at the University of Washington from 1990 to 1993. As a member of the Eöt-Wash Group, named in honor of [[Loránd Eötvös]], Gundlach did research in experimental gravitational physics. With his colleagues he searched for the confirmation or refutation of a hypothetical [[fifth force]], which might cause deviations from Newtonian gravity, depend on material properties and violate the equivalence principle. At the University of Washington, Gundlach was from 1993 to 1998 an assistant professor and from 1998 to 2004 an associate professor with promotion to full professor in 2004. He has been a member of the University of Washington's Center for Experimental Nuclear Physics and Astrophysics since its founding in 2000.<ref>{{cite web|title=Center for Experimental Nuclear Physics and Astrophysics (CENPA)|website=University of Washington|url=https://www.npl.washington.edu}}</ref>

In the Eöt-Wash Group, Gundlach built torsion balances to test the [[equivalence principle]], test Newton's law of gravity at short distances and measure the strength of gravity. The latter measurement consisted of an instrument that held a thin plate by a tungsten filament inside a high vacuum. This torsion balance was mounted on a turntable, inside an outer turntable with two spherical field masses facing each other. Compared to previous experiments with dumbbell-shaped pendulums on a torsion wire, the Gundlach's measurement was not limited by how well the mass distribution of the  pendulum was known. Additionally, the inner turntable was rotated in feedback exactly so that the torsion thread was not twisted, despite the gravitational deceleration and acceleration by the masses on the outer turntable. The inner turntable's regulated rotation eliminated uncertainties from the inelasticity of the torsion thread which had plagued previous measurements. In another experiment, Gundlach and his colleagues conducted the first test of the <math>\frac {1}{r^2}</math> form of the gravitational force down to values of <math>r</math> in the 50 micron range. In this range, according to various large extradimensional theories by [[Nima Arkani-Hamed]] and other string theorists, possibilities begin to occur for discrepancies caused by 4''D'' gravity (or even higher dimensional gravitational theories) without a [[cosmological constant]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/S0370-2693(00)00359-2|title=A small cosmological constant from a large extra dimension |year=2000 |last1=Arkani-Hamed |first1=Nima |last2=Dimopoulos |first2=Savas |last3=Kaloper |first3=Nemanja |last4=Sundrum |first4=Raman |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=480 |issue=1–2 |pages=193–199 |arxiv=hep-th/0001197 |bibcode=2000PhLB..480..193A |s2cid=17949423 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1155/2011/189379|doi-access=free |title=Gravity and Large Extra Dimensions |year=2011 |last1=Satheeshkumar |first1=V. H. |last2=Suresh |first2=P. K. |journal=Advances in Astronomy |volume=2011 |pages=1–12 |arxiv=hep-th/0606194 |bibcode=2011AdAst2011E..14S }}</ref>

In 2000 Gundlach succeeded in measuring the [[Gravitational constant|gravitational constant <math>G</math>]] with a new torsion balance technique that he had developed. Since 2006, the [[CODATA]] value for <math>G</math> is mostly based on this measurement.

He is a member of [[LIGO]] and [[Laser Interferometer Space Antenna|LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna)]], the planned satellite-based laser interferometric gravitational-wave detector, and has performed ultra-weak force measurements with the laser interferometers for gravitational-wave detection.

Since about 2002 Gundlach has done research in [[biophysics]]. In his bio-research he has pioneered [[nanopore sequencing]] technology. In 2008 his group demonstrated that a mutated version of the biological nanopore MspA could pass DNA and that it had the desired shape to identify individual nucleotides in single-stranded DNA.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1073/pnas.0807514106|title=Single-molecule DNA detection with an engineered MspA protein nanopore |year=2008 |last1=Butler |first1=Tom Z. |last2=Pavlenok |first2=Mikhail |last3=Derrington |first3=Ian M. |last4=Niederweis |first4=Michael |last5=Gundlach |first5=Jens H. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=105 |issue=52 |pages=20647–20652 |pmid=19098105 |pmc=2634888 |bibcode=2008PNAS..10520647B |doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2012 The Gundlach group demonstrated functional nanopore sequencing using MspA and an enzyme to control the passage of the DNA through the pore.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1038/nbt.2171|title=Reading DNA at single-nucleotide resolution with a mutant MspA nanopore and phi29 DNA polymerase |year=2012 |last1=Manrao |first1=Elizabeth A. |last2=Derrington |first2=Ian M. |last3=Laszlo |first3=Andrew H. |last4=Langford |first4=Kyle W. |last5=Hopper |first5=Matthew K. |last6=Gillgren |first6=Nathaniel |last7=Pavlenok |first7=Mikhail |last8=Niederweis |first8=Michael |last9=Gundlach |first9=Jens H. |journal=Nature Biotechnology |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=349–353 |pmid=22446694 |pmc=3757088 }}</ref>  His group is now using their nanopore technology as a single-molecule tool to study how enzymes process along DNA or RNA.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1038/nbt.3357|title= Subangstrom single-molecule measurements of motor proteins using a nanopore |year=2015 |last1= Derrington Laszlo |first1= Ian M. |last2=Craig |first2= Jonathan M.  |last3=Stava|first3=Eric |last4=Laszlo |first4=Andrew H. |last5=Ross |first5= Brian C. |last6=Brinkerhoff |first6=Henry |last7=Tickman|first7=Benjamin I. |last8=Ronaghi |first8=Mostafa| last9=Mandell |first9=Jeffrey G. | last10=Gunderson |first10=Kevin L. |last11=Gundlach |first11=Jens H. |journal= Nature Biotechnology  |volume=10 |issue=47 |pages=1073–1075|pmid= 26414351 |pmc= 4915380 }} </ref>     

Gundlach received in 2001 the [[Francis M. Pipkin Award]] of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).<ref>{{cite web|title=2001 Francis M. Pipkin Award Recipient, Jens H. Gundlach|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Gundlach&first_nm=Jens&year=2001}}</ref> In 2009 he was elected a fellow of the APS in recognition of his "contributions to precision mechanical measurements and our quantitative understanding of the strength of gravity".<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2009&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Washington}} (search on year=2009 and institution=University of Washington)</ref> In 2021 he received, jointly with Eric Adelberger and Blayne Heckel, the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] for "precision fundamental measurements that test our understanding of gravity, probe the nature of [[dark energy]], and establish limits on couplings to [[dark matter]]."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/60|title=Breakthrough Prize – Winners Of The 2021 Breakthrough Prizes In Life Sciences, Fundamental Physics And Mathematics Announced|website=breakthroughprize.org}}</ref>

He is married and has three children.{{cn|date=July 2023}}
